Every Saturday morning, Tomás rode his bicycle to the Oak Hill Animal Shelter, where he walked the dogs and scrubbed the food bowls. Most of the dogs leaped against their gates whenever he passed, barking and wagging as if he were a celebrity. One dog, however, never moved at all. She was a thin brown mutt named Pepper, and she spent every day pressed into the farthest corner of her kennel.

"Pepper was discovered living under a bridge," explained Ms. Okafor, the shelter director. "Nobody knows what happened to her before that, and she doesn't trust people yet."

Tomás tried every idea he could imagine. He called her name in a cheerful voice, offered treats through the bars, and even squeaked a rubber chicken. Each time, Pepper only trembled and turned her face toward the wall.

After three discouraging weeks, Tomás was ready to quit. "She just doesn't like me," he told Ms. Okafor.

Ms. Okafor smiled patiently. "Maybe you're trying too hard. Imagine a stranger running toward you and shouting your name. Would that make you feel safe?"

Tomás remembered his first day at his new school last fall. Everyone had crowded around him with questions, and all he had wanted to do was disappear.

The following Saturday, Tomás tried a different approach. He brought a library book, sat on the floor outside Pepper's kennel, and read aloud in a low, quiet voice. He did not look at her, and he did not offer any treats; he simply read.

For the first hour, nothing happened, and the next Saturday was the same. On the third Saturday, however, Tomás heard a soft scraping sound. From the corner of his eye, he noticed Pepper creep a few inches closer before she lay down with her nose resting against the bars.

Tomás continued reading, but his heart was pounding like a drum.

By the end of the month, Pepper was waiting at the front of her kennel whenever Tomás arrived, and her tail swept back and forth across the floor. When he finally opened the gate, she climbed into his lap as if she had always belonged there.

Ms. Okafor shook her head in amazement and asked how he had done it.

Tomás scratched Pepper behind the ears. "I stopped asking her to trust me," he said, "and just gave her time."
stem: Which sentence best states the theme of the story?
choices: Shelter dogs are happiest when people give them lots of treats.
Trust often grows slowly when someone is patient and gentle.
Reading out loud is the best way to train any animal.
People should give up on a goal after a few weeks of trying.
explanation: Pepper begins to trust Tomás only after he stops pushing and quietly gives her time, as his last line says. The other choices are not supported; treats and squeaky toys did not work, and Tomás succeeds because he does not give up.

Anika had been a reporter for the Lincoln Ledger, her school's newspaper, for only a month when she stumbled onto the biggest news of the year. She was waiting in the cafeteria line when she overheard Mr. Haddad, the head cook, talking to a helper.

"After this week, we're finished with the Friday pizza," he said.

Anika nearly dropped her tray, because Pizza Friday was the most popular day at Lincoln Elementary. That afternoon she wrote an article with the headline "No More Pizza Fridays!" The editor, a sixth grader named Marcus, loved it, and the story appeared on the front page the next morning.

By lunchtime, the whole school was in an uproar. Fourth graders made protest signs, and a group of fifth graders started a petition that collected two hundred names. Anika felt proud, since her first big story had everyone talking.

Then Mr. Haddad stopped her in the hallway, looking puzzled rather than angry.

"Anika, I read your article," he said. "We aren't getting rid of pizza. We're getting rid of the frozen pizza, and starting next month, my team is going to make it fresh with homemade dough and real vegetables."

Anika's face grew hot with embarrassment. She had heard only half of the conversation, and she had never asked Mr. Haddad a single question.

She hurried to the newspaper office to find Marcus and announced that they needed to fix the mistake.

Marcus shrugged. "Everyone will forget about it in a week. If we print a correction, people will decide the Ledger can't be trusted."

Anika thought about the petition, the signs, and the younger students who were truly upset. "If we don't fix it," she said slowly, "then they really shouldn't trust us."

That evening she wrote a new article. This time she interviewed Mr. Haddad for twenty minutes, asking about the new recipe, the cost, and when the change would begin. At the top of the page, she added a note: "Last week the Ledger reported that pizza was being removed from the menu, which was wrong, and I am sorry."

The next Friday, students lined up early for the first homemade pizza. While Anika waited, a fourth grader tapped her on the shoulder and asked whether she was the reporter who had written the correction.

When Anika nodded, the girl grinned. "I'm going to read everything you write from now on."
stem: What is the main problem in the story?
choices: Mr. Haddad decides to stop serving pizza at Lincoln Elementary.
Marcus refuses to let Anika write for the school newspaper.
Anika publishes a story that is wrong because she did not check her facts.
The fifth graders cannot collect enough names for their petition.
explanation: Anika writes "No More Pizza Fridays!" after hearing only half of a conversation, and the whole story is about how she deals with that mistake. Mr. Haddad never planned to stop serving pizza.

Long ago, in a green valley between two mountains, an elderly farmer named Bao divided his land between his two sons. To Kiet, the elder, he gave the eastern field, and to Lan, the younger, he gave the western field. "Use the soil wisely," Bao told them, "and it will feed you for the rest of your lives."

Kiet wasted no time. That very spring he planted melons, which grew quickly and sold for a handsome price at the market. By autumn his pockets jingled with coins, and he purchased an elegant new coat.

Lan did something that puzzled everyone in the village. He planted rows of tiny walnut trees that were no taller than his knee. Because walnut trees require many years to produce nuts, Lan had nothing to sell for a long time. He earned a little money by repairing fences for his neighbors, and he wore the same patched shirt year after year.

Kiet scoffed at his younger brother. "You are planting for an old man, but I am planting for today."

Lan only smiled and continued watering his saplings.

Eight summers passed, and then came a terrible year when no rain fell at all. The river shrank to a muddy trickle, and the sun baked the valley floor until it cracked. Kiet's melons withered on their vines before they could ripen. He planted a second crop, but it died as well, and by winter his coins had disappeared and his elegant coat had worn thin.

On the western side of the valley, however, the walnut trees stood tall and healthy. Over the years their roots had grown deep enough to reach water far beneath the dry ground. That autumn the branches sagged with nuts, and Lan filled sack after sack.

One frosty evening Kiet knocked on his brother's door. He stared at his boots and could not find any words to say.

Lan placed a heavy sack in his brother's arms. "Father gave us two fields," he said, "but he raised us as one family."

The next spring, the brothers worked side by side. In the eastern field they planted melons to sell that summer, and along its edges they planted walnut trees for the years to come. Kiet dug every hole himself, and this time he did not complain about waiting.
stem: Which lesson does the story teach?
choices: It is always better to grow fruit than to grow trees.
Hard work never matters when the weather is bad.
Planning for the future can be wiser than seeking quick rewards.
Older brothers should make all the decisions for a family.
explanation: Kiet's quick melon profits disappear in the drought, while Lan's slow-growing walnut trees survive and feed both brothers. In the end even Kiet plants trees "for the years to come."

Make a fist and squeeze it as hard as you can. Now open and squeeze it again, about once every second. Your hand will probably grow tired within a few minutes. Yet a muscle about the size of that fist has been squeezing inside your chest every second of your life, and it never takes a break. That muscle is your heart.

The heart is the center of the circulatory system, the body system that moves blood to every part of you. Blood carries oxygen from the air you breathe and nutrients from the food you eat. Every cell in your body needs these supplies to stay alive and do its job. Blood also carries away wastes, such as carbon dioxide, that cells must get rid of.

Blood travels through tubes called blood vessels. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, while veins carry blood back to it. Between them are capillaries, tiny vessels thinner than a hair. In the capillaries, oxygen and nutrients pass out of the blood and into the cells, and wastes pass in. If you could lay all of your blood vessels end to end, they would stretch around Earth more than twice.

The heart itself has four rooms, or chambers, and the two on the right side pump blood to the lungs. There the blood drops off carbon dioxide, which you breathe out, and picks up fresh oxygen. The blood then returns to the left side of the heart. The left side pumps this oxygen-rich blood out to the rest of the body. Because the left side has the harder job, its walls are thicker and stronger.

Each time the heart squeezes, it pushes a wave of blood through the arteries. You can feel this wave, called your pulse, in your wrist or neck. When you run or jump, your muscles need more oxygen, so your heart beats faster to deliver it.

Like any muscle, the heart grows stronger with exercise. Playing outside, riding a bike, and dancing all give your heart a workout. Eating nutritious foods and getting enough sleep help, too. Take care of your heart, and it will keep working hard for you.

The Grand Canyon in Arizona is more than a mile deep in some places. Standing at its edge, you might guess that a giant once carved it with a shovel. The real sculptors were much smaller and much slower: water, wind, and ice working for millions of years.

Scientists use two words to describe how the land changes. Weathering is the breaking down of rock into smaller pieces. Erosion is the moving of those pieces from one place to another. Weathering makes the pieces, and erosion carries them away.

Weathering happens in several ways. In cold places, rain seeps into small cracks in rock. When the temperature drops, the water freezes and expands, pushing the crack a little wider. After the ice melts, more water flows in. Over many winters, this cycle can split a boulder in two. Plants cause weathering, too. A tree root growing into a crack acts like a slowly opening wedge. Even the acid in rainwater can dissolve some kinds of rock, such as limestone.

Once rock has been broken apart, erosion goes to work. Moving water is the most powerful force of erosion on Earth. Rivers pick up sand and pebbles and tumble them downstream, scraping the riverbed as they go. That is exactly how the Colorado River cut the Grand Canyon, grinding a little deeper year after year. Wind can also cause erosion, especially in deserts, where it blasts sand against rocks. In very cold regions, enormous sheets of ice called glaciers creep downhill and drag huge rocks along with them.

The pieces that erosion carries away do not vanish. Eventually, the water or wind slows down and drops them. This process is called deposition. A river that empties into the sea may leave behind so much mud and sand that it builds new land. The area of land that forms at the mouth of a river is called a delta.

Weathering and erosion can cause problems for people. They can wash away farm soil and weaken roads and bridges. Farmers plant grass and trees to hold the soil in place, and towns build walls to protect their beaches. Still, these forces never stop, slowly reshaping the land beneath our feet.

passage:
Imagine a classroom where one student made all the rules, decided who broke them, and chose every punishment. That student would have a lot of power, and the others would have very little say. The people who wrote the United States Constitution in 1787 worried about this kind of problem. They had just fought a war to escape the rule of a king, and they did not want any one person or group to become too powerful.

Their solution was to divide the national government into three parts, called branches. Each branch has its own job.

The legislative branch makes the laws. It is called Congress, and it has two parts, the Senate and the House of Representatives. Members of Congress are elected by the people of each state. When they want to create a new law, they write a plan called a bill. Both parts of Congress must vote to approve it.

The executive branch carries out the laws. The president leads this branch. After Congress passes a bill, the president can sign it into law. The president also commands the military and works with leaders of other countries. Many departments help the president, such as the ones that manage schools, farms, and national parks.

The judicial branch explains the laws. It includes the Supreme Court and many lower courts. Judges decide what laws mean and whether they follow the rules in the Constitution. If the Supreme Court decides that a law breaks those rules, the law can no longer be used.

The writers of the Constitution also gave each branch ways to limit the others. This idea is called checks and balances. For example, the president can veto, or reject, a bill that Congress has passed. However, Congress can still turn that bill into a law if two-thirds of its members vote for it again. The president chooses judges for the Supreme Court, but the Senate must agree to each choice.

Checks and balances can make the government move slowly, because the branches often have to work together and compromise. Yet that is exactly what the writers wanted. By sharing power, the three branches help protect the rights of every citizen.

They needed more jobs for people who had fought in the war.
They did not want any one person or group to become too powerful.
They wanted the government to make decisions as quickly as possible.
explanation: The first paragraph explains that the writers had escaped the rule of a king and "did not want any one person or group to become too powerful."

The judicial branch explains the laws. It includes the Supreme Court and many lower courts. Judges decide what laws mean and whether they follow the rules in the Constitution. If the Supreme Court decides that a law breaks those rules, the law can no longer be used.

The writers of the Constitution also gave each branch ways to limit the others. This idea is called checks and balances. stem: The words ERUPT, INTERRUPT, and RUPTURE all share the Latin root RUPT. What does RUPT most likely mean?
explanation: A volcano erupts when it breaks open, and you interrupt when you break into a conversation, so RUPT means "break."

stem: MANUAL, MANUSCRIPT, and MANUFACTURE all contain the Latin root MANU. What does MANU most likely mean?
explanation: A manual task is done by hand, and a manuscript was once written by hand, so MANU means "hand."

stem: PEDAL, PEDESTRIAN, and CENTIPEDE all contain the Latin root PED. What does PED mean?
explanation: You push a pedal with your foot, a pedestrian travels on foot, and a centipede seems to have a hundred feet, so PED means "foot."

stem: What does the prefix SEMI- mean in the word SEMICIRCLE?
explanation: A semicircle is half of a circle. SEMI- means "half" or "partly," as in semifinal.

stem: What does the suffix -IST mean in the words ARTIST and SCIENTIST?
choices: a person who does or studies something
explanation: An artist is a person who makes art, and a scientist is a person who studies science, so -IST means "a person who does or studies something."

stem: What does the suffix -WARD mean in the words HOMEWARD and UPWARD?
explanation: Homeward means "toward home," and upward means "toward a higher place," so -WARD means "in the direction of."

stem: What does the prefix NON- mean in the word NONFICTION?
explanation: Nonfiction is writing that is not made up. The prefix NON- means "not," as in nonstop and nonsense.

stem: Which word is a SYNONYM for VERTICAL?
explanation: Something vertical goes straight up and down, so UPRIGHT is a synonym. FLAT is closer to horizontal, its opposite.

stem: Which word is a SYNONYM for SWIFT?
explanation: SWIFT means moving with great speed, so QUICK is a synonym.

stem: Which word is an ANTONYM for SHRINK?
explanation: To shrink is to become smaller, and to grow is to become larger. DWINDLE is a synonym for SHRINK.

stem: Which word is an ANTONYM for ARTIFICIAL?
explanation: Something artificial is made by people, while something natural comes from nature. FAKE is close in meaning to ARTIFICIAL.

stem: Read the sentence: "After the storm passed, the floodwater began to RECEDE, and the streets slowly dried out." What does RECEDE mean?
explanation: The streets "slowly dried out," which tells you the water was going away. RECEDE means to move back or become lower.

stem: Read the sentence: "Grandma is very FRUGAL; she reuses gift wrap and never buys anything she does not need." What does FRUGAL mean?
explanation: Reusing gift wrap and buying only what she needs are clues that FRUGAL means careful not to waste money.

stem: Read the sentence: "A fallen tree was an OBSTACLE on the trail, so the hikers had to climb over it." What is an OBSTACLE?
explanation: The hikers had to climb over the tree to keep going, so an OBSTACLE is something that blocks your way.

stem: Read the sentence: "The twins' handwriting is nearly IDENTICAL, so even their teacher cannot tell whose paper is whose." What does IDENTICAL mean?
explanation: The teacher cannot tell the papers apart, which shows that IDENTICAL means exactly the same.

stem: Read the sentence: "The little stream MEANDERED through the meadow, curving back and forth like a ribbon." What does MEANDERED mean?
explanation: The clue "curving back and forth like a ribbon" shows that MEANDERED means followed a slow, winding path.

stem: In which sentence does FAIR mean "treating everyone equally"?
choices: We rode the Ferris wheel at the county FAIR.
Tomorrow the weather will be FAIR and sunny.
The referee made a FAIR call, so neither team complained.
The baby has FAIR hair and blue eyes.
explanation: A fair call by a referee treats both teams the same way. In the other sentences FAIR means an outdoor festival, light in color, and clear weather.

stem: In which sentence does BARK mean "the outer covering of a tree"?
choices: The rough BARK of the oak scraped my hands.
The seals BARK as they swim near the dock.
I heard a loud BARK from the yard next door.
Our puppy will BARK at the mail carrier.
explanation: Only in the first sentence is BARK something on a tree that can scrape your hands. In the others it is the sound an animal makes.

stem: Read the sentence: "The hikers filled their bottles with cold, clear water from a SPRING beside the trail." What does SPRING mean in this sentence?
choices: a place where water flows up from the ground
a coil of metal that bounces back
explanation: The hikers get water from it beside the trail, so SPRING here means a natural source of water coming out of the ground.

stem: Read the sentence: "Before dinner, Dad asked me to SET the table." What does SET mean in this sentence?
choices: a group of things that belong together
explanation: When you set the table, you arrange plates, cups, and silverware on it for a meal. The other choices are different meanings of SET.

stem: Kendra joined the soccer team, the school play, and the chess club in the same week, and now she has no free time. Her dad says she BIT OFF MORE THAN SHE COULD CHEW. What does this mean?
choices: She ate too much food at lunch.
She took on more than she could handle.
She refused to try anything new.
explanation: Joining three activities at once left Kendra with no free time. The idiom means taking on more work or responsibility than you can manage.

stem: Marco promised to keep the surprise party a secret, but he SPILLED THE BEANS at breakfast. What does SPILLED THE BEANS mean?
choices: made a mess at the table
explanation: Marco was supposed to keep a secret, so SPILLED THE BEANS means he revealed it before he should have.

stem: When Ruby said the story was really about friendship, the teacher smiled and said, "You HIT THE NAIL ON THE HEAD." What did the teacher mean?
explanation: The teacher smiles because Ruby found the true theme. HIT THE NAIL ON THE HEAD means to say something exactly right.

stem: My cousins live far away, so we see them only ONCE IN A BLUE MOON. What does ONCE IN A BLUE MOON mean?
explanation: Because the cousins live far away, the family seldom sees them. ONCE IN A BLUE MOON means very rarely.

stem: What does the saying DON'T JUDGE A BOOK BY ITS COVER mean?
choices: Don't decide what someone or something is like based only on how it looks.
Books with plain covers are usually the most interesting.
Take good care of library books so the covers stay clean.
Always read the whole book before you write a report.
explanation: The saying warns that outward appearance does not always show what is inside or what a person is really like.

stem: What does the saying TWO HEADS ARE BETTER THAN ONE mean?
choices: People should always work alone to avoid arguments.
It is better to have two teachers in every classroom.
Thinking about a problem twice is a waste of time.
Two people working together can often solve a problem better than one person alone.
explanation: The saying means that sharing ideas with another person often leads to a better solution.

stem: Complete the analogy. STETHOSCOPE is to DOCTOR as HAMMER is to ______.
explanation: A stethoscope is a tool a doctor uses, and a hammer is a tool a carpenter uses. The relationship is tool to worker.

stem: Complete the analogy. FOAL is to HORSE as CUB is to ______.
explanation: A foal is a young horse, and a cub is a young bear. The relationship is young animal to adult animal.

stem: Which word shows the STRONGEST degree of happiness?
explanation: All four words describe happiness, but OVERJOYED means extremely happy, while CONTENT, PLEASED, and GLAD are milder.

stem: Your teacher asks you to PARAPHRASE a paragraph from your science book. What should you do?
choices: restate its ideas in your own words
read it aloud to a partner
explanation: To PARAPHRASE means to explain the same ideas using your own words instead of the author's exact words.

stem:

"When the power went out, I ______ a shower."
explanation: The past progressive WAS TAKING shows an action that was in progress when another past event, the power going out, interrupted it.

explanation: BLOW is an irregular verb; its simple past form is BLEW. BLOWED is not a word, and BLOWN needs a helping verb.

"Have you ever ______ a horse?"
explanation: After the helping verb HAVE, use the past participle. The past participle of RIDE is RIDDEN.

stem:

"The flock of geese ______ south every fall."
explanation: The subject is FLOCK, a singular collective noun, so it takes the singular verb FLIES. "Of geese" is a phrase that does not change the subject.

stem:
Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence.
"Mathematics ______ my favorite subject this year."
explanation: MATHEMATICS ends in -s but is a singular subject, so it takes the singular verb IS.

stem:
Choose the verb that correctly completes the sentence.
"There ______ three baby birds in the nest outside my window."
explanation: In a sentence that begins with THERE, the subject comes after the verb. The subject BIRDS is plural, so the verb is ARE.

stem:
Choose the pronoun that correctly completes the sentence.
"Ms. Lee asked Sam and ______ to carry the boxes to the gym."
explanation: The pronoun is an object of the verb ASKED, so the object pronoun ME is correct. Try it alone: "Ms. Lee asked me."

stem:
Choose the pronoun that correctly completes the sentence.
"The campers set up the tents by ______."
explanation: THEMSELVES is the correct reflexive pronoun for a plural subject. THEIRSELVES, THEMSELF, and THEIRSELF are not standard English.

stem:
Choose the pronoun that correctly completes the sentence.
"Every student must bring ______ own water bottle on the field trip."
explanation: EVERY STUDENT is singular, so in formal school English the pronoun is HIS OR HER. ITS is used for things, and OUR does not match the antecedent.

stem:
Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence.
"Of all the planets in our solar system, Jupiter is the ______."
explanation: When comparing three or more things, use the superlative form. For a short adjective like LARGE, add -EST.

stem:
Choose the words that correctly complete the sentence.
"Everyone agreed that the movie was ______ than the book."
explanation: For a long adjective like EXCITING, use MORE to compare two things. Never add -ER to a word that already uses MORE.

stem:

"That was the ______ snowstorm our town has had in fifty years."
explanation: BAD is irregular: bad, worse, worst. The sentence compares this storm with all the storms in fifty years, so the superlative WORST is correct.

stem:
Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence.
"The choir sang so ______ that the audience stood up and cheered."
explanation: The word describes how the choir sang, a verb, so it must be the adverb BEAUTIFULLY.

stem:

"Diego studied hard, and he did ______ on his science test."
explanation: WELL is an adverb that describes how Diego did. GOOD is an adjective and should not describe a verb.

stem: Which group of words is a complete sentence?

Running down the hallway after the bell.
The children laughed at the clown.
Because the bus was late this morning.
explanation: A complete sentence needs a subject and a verb and must express a complete thought. The other choices are fragments.

stem: Which of these is a run-on sentence?
choices: The rain stopped; we went outside to play.
The rain stopped, and we went outside to play.
After the rain stopped, we went outside to play.
The rain stopped we went outside to play.
explanation: A run-on joins two complete sentences with no punctuation or conjunction. The other choices join the clauses correctly with a comma and AND, a dependent clause, or a semicolon.

stem: Which sentence correctly uses a semicolon?
choices: Maria loves; to swim her brother prefers to hike.
Maria loves to swim her brother; prefers to hike.
Maria loves to swim; her brother prefers to hike.
Maria; loves to swim her brother prefers to hike.
explanation: A semicolon can join two complete sentences that are closely related. Each side of the semicolon must be a complete thought.

stem: Which sentence correctly uses commas to set off an appositive (a phrase that renames a noun)?
choices: My neighbor a retired pilot, taught me how to fold paper airplanes.
My neighbor, a retired pilot taught me how to fold paper airplanes.
My, neighbor a retired pilot taught me how to fold paper airplanes.
My neighbor, a retired pilot, taught me how to fold paper airplanes.
explanation: The phrase "a retired pilot" renames "my neighbor," so it needs a comma before it and a comma after it.

stem: Which sentence uses commas correctly with city and state names?
choices: We moved from Tucson, Arizona, to Portland, Maine, last year.
We moved from Tucson, Arizona to Portland Maine, last year.
We moved from, Tucson, Arizona to Portland, Maine last year.
We moved from Tucson Arizona, to Portland Maine, last year.
explanation: Put a comma between a city and its state, and another comma after the state when the sentence continues.

explanation: WOMEN is a plural that does not end in -s, so you add an apostrophe and -s to make it possessive: WOMEN'S.

stem:
Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence.
"The cat licked ______ paw after dinner."
explanation: ITS (with no apostrophe) is a possessive pronoun. IT'S is a contraction that means "it is."

stem: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
choices: Last Thanksgiving, my Family drove to the Pacific ocean.
last Thanksgiving, my family drove to the Pacific Ocean.
Last thanksgiving, my family drove to the pacific ocean.
Last Thanksgiving, my family drove to the Pacific Ocean.

stem: Which sentence punctuates the dialogue correctly?

stem:
Choose the conjunction that best completes the sentence.
"We cannot go camping this weekend ______ the rain stops."
explanation: UNLESS means "if not": the camping trip cannot happen if the rain does not stop. The other conjunctions do not make sense here.

stem: Which sentence lists the adjectives in the correct order?
choices: She keeps her letters in a wooden old small box.
She keeps her letters in an old wooden small box.
She keeps her letters in a small old wooden box.
She keeps her letters in a wooden small old box.
explanation: In English, adjectives usually go in this order: size, then age, then material. So the correct order is SMALL OLD WOODEN.
